description: I’m an Electrical & Computer Engineering student at the University of Washington, working in embedded systems, sensors and data analysis. For NASA Space Apps 2026 I built Marswalk, a tablet app that helps the first astronauts on Mars plan spacewalks and respond to dust storms and radiation, using real NASA terrain, weather and radiation data.
summary: Marswalk is a tablet app for the first astronauts on Mars. Earth is 4 to 24 minutes away, so when a dust storm or solar radiation event hits during a spacewalk, the crew must decide on their own. Marswalk layers real NASA terrain, weather and radiation data onto one 3D map of Jezero crater. It plans each walk by distance, time and radiation dose. When a dust front is detected, it gives the crew a countdown. It compares the shortest way to shelter with the option most likely to succeed across 2,000 simulated storms. It also traces the storm through air pressure to the astronaut’s remaining dose limit. Bases share storm reports, so the first base a storm hits warns the rest of the planet days ahead. This answers the challenge with a map built around one person on one walk, not a region. Storms on Mars can’t be forecast, so the way to be ready is to practise. Crews rehearse real storms in the habitat, then carry the same numbers outside on the helmet visor.
details:
What it does and how it works
Marswalk is a tablet app for the first astronauts on Mars. It follows one astronaut, Maya, on a walk at Jezero crater. Before she leaves, the app plans her route on real NASA terrain and shows its distance, walking time, slope and radiation dose. During the walk, weather stations detect an approaching dust front, and the app gives her a countdown. It then offers two options: the shortest way to shelter, and the option with the best odds across 2,000 simulated storms, where front speed and walking pace are uncertain. In our demo the best option is a staged rover nearby: Maya shelters there, waits out the gusts and drives home. In the habitat, crews rehearse storms on real data. Outside, the same numbers appear on the helmet visor.

Behind this are four models, each fitted to published NASA mission data:

  • Dust front: moves at 25 m/s, as measured at Jezero in January 2022 (Sánchez-Lavega et al. 2025). Once two stations have seen it, the speed estimate narrows to ±2 m/s.
  • Planet-wide storms: a spreading model fitted to the 2018 and 2022 storms. Bases share only the times the storm reached them, and the app infers where it started and when it will reach other bases. Tested on the 2018 storm, it predicted Gale at 14.7–16.4 sols after three reports; the true value was 15.5.
  • Radiation: dose rises as air pressure falls, about 0.13 µGy/day per pascal (Guo et al. 2015, fitted to Curiosity RAD). A storm makes the daily pressure swing 2–3× larger (Sánchez-Lavega et al. 2023). Solar-particle events are flagged with a published nowcast rule (Löwe et al. 2025).
  • Dose limit: every walk is tracked against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit, and Maya’s remaining dose appears on her visor.

Benefits
Earth is 4 to 24 minutes away, so mission control can’t steer a walk in real time. Marswalk puts the data the crew needs in one place: where to go, how long it takes, what it costs in dose, and where to hide. It gives a clear choice with odds, not a wall of numbers.

Intended impact
Storms on Mars can’t be forecast, so the way to be ready is to practise. Marswalk lets crews rehearse real storms before they go and carry the same tool outside. Mission planners can use it as a sandbox: move stations and bases, replay real storms, and see how a layout turns into minutes or days of warning.

Tools and languages

  • JavaScript, three.js and Vite for the 3D app and helmet visor.
  • Python (GDAL, NumPy, Matplotlib) to process terrain, weather and radiation data and draw our model figures.
  • Automated Node tests for routing, the storm model and the radiation model.
  • GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions for deployment.
  • No hardware.

How it is creative
Most Mars maps show regions or the whole planet. Marswalk is built around one person on one walk. It follows a storm all the way from the first station that sees it, through air pressure and radiation, to Maya’s remaining dose. It also treats every base as a weather sensor, so the first base a storm hits warns the rest of the planet days ahead.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about results. Our own model shows a dust storm adds only about 0.3 µSv to a walk through the pressure effect. A solar event like May 2024 would add about 1.6 mSv in two hours. We report both: for dust, the crew’s problem is time; for radiation, it is solar storms.
  • Uncertainty. Front speed and walking pace are uncertain, so we use Monte Carlo odds instead of a single estimate. Bases infer the storm’s origin; they are not told it.
  • What we do not claim. No weather station network exists on Mars yet. The storm model replays and infers; it does not forecast. Our 20 m terrain cannot show single boulders. Every value in the app is labelled measured, replay, model, assumed or scenario.
  • Usability under stress. The decision dialog shows only two options, with the research folded away. The visor shows only what Maya needs while walking.
